autor: Nikephoros Bryennios the Younger (c. 1080–1137), Caesar, husband of Anna Komnene and grandson of the general of 1071; Hyle Historias ('Materials for History'), written in the 1120s–1130s for the empress Eirene Doukaina, daughter of Andronikos Doukas
quelle: Nicephori Bryennii Commentarii, ed. August Meineke, Corpus Scriptorum Historiae Byzantinae (Bonn: Weber, 1836), Book I, chapters 12–25, pp. 35–55, bound with Kinnamos. Internet Archive, Google scan ioanniscinnamie00meingoog (printed page n = page image n+462), checked against a second scan (ioanniscinnamie01meingoog). Public domain.
hinweis: The Greek is Meineke's text, set from two independent OCRs and read against the page images line by line; the printer's curly theta is set as θ and hyphenations are joined. The lacuna Possinus marked at the start of chapter 20 is kept as asterisks. Meineke's apparatus is not carried, except in notes. The units are his chapters or parts of them; each shows its Bonn page and line range. The English is this site's working translation (CC0); Possinus' facing Latin was consulted. Bryennios copies Psellos in whole sentences and adds the family's details: his grandfather's counsel and wounds, Andronikos Doukas' virtues and his protest against the blinding, the trial of Anna Dalassene.

sections.blurb: The family's version, written two generations later for Eirene Doukaina: Alexios Komnenos sent home in tears; the author's grandfather and Trachaneiotes advising the emperor to wait at Theodosiopolis; a false report that the sultan was fleeing; Basilakes' rash charge and the grandfather's wounds; the order of battle, with Andronikos Doukas, 'not at all friendly to the emperor', in the rear; the eunuch Taranges' ambushes; 'at once those of the rearguard withdrew too'; the emperor taken, and the pearl called the Orphan lost.

units.titel: 12. Alexios sent back to his mother
units.orig: ἀπάρας οὖν ἐκεῖθεν τῆς πρὸς τὸν βασιλέα φερούσης ἥπτετο, καὶ δὴ φθάνει τοῦτον περὶ τὸ Δορύλαιον σκηνοῦντα καὶ τὸν στρατὸν συναγείραντα. ὁ δὲ τοῦτον ἰδὼν καὶ ἐν ἀναμνήσει τοῦ πάθους γενόμενος δακρύειν τε ἤρξατο καὶ περὶ τῆς ἐκείνου μητρὸς ἐπυνθάνετο. καὶ τέλος βιάζεται τοῦτον πρὸς τὴν μητέρα παλινοστῆσαι, τοῦτο φράσας ὡς οὐ καλόν ἐστι ταύτην ἐπὶ τοσούτῳ μεγέθει πάθους καταλιπεῖν ἀπαράκλητον, τῷ πάθει πάθος προσθέντας τῷ ἐκείνου θανάτῳ τὴν σὴν ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἀποδημίαν. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ὁ βασιλεύς. ὁ δ᾽ ἐπειρᾶτο προσμένειν καὶ ξυνέπεσθαί οἱ κατὰ βαρβάρων στρατεύοντι. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα λέγων τὸν βασιλέα οὐκ ἔπειθε· καὶ ἄκοντα γὰρ τοῦτον ἐπαναζεῦξαι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα παρεσκεύασεν. ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀπῄει, ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς πρόσω χωρῶν τὰς Ῥωμαϊκὰς δυνάμεις συνήθροιζε καὶ πρὸς τὸν πόλεμον αὐτῷ ἐξηρτύετο.
units.en: So Alexios set out from there and took the road leading to the emperor, and reached him while he was camped near Dorylaion and had gathered the army. The emperor, seeing him and reminded of the loss, began to weep and asked about his mother. In the end he compelled him to go back to his mother, saying that it was not right to leave her without comfort in so great a grief, adding grief to grief: 'your long absence to his death'. So said the emperor. Alexios tried to stay and follow him on campaign against the barbarians; but for all he said he did not persuade the emperor, who made him return to his mother against his will. So he went away, and the emperor, advancing, gathered the Roman forces and prepared the war.
units.note: Alexios Komnenos, the future emperor Alexios I, was fourteen; his elder brother Manuel had just died (Att. 1070 [1], [5]). The author, the younger Nikephoros Bryennios, married Alexios' daughter Anna Komnene and wrote this history at the request of Alexios' wife Eirene Doukaina: a Doukas and a Komnenos stand behind every page.

units.titel: 13. The council in Cappadocia: advance or wait?
units.orig: 13. Γενόμενος δὲ περὶ τὴν Καππαδοκῶν τοὺς ἀρίστους ἅμα τῶν στρατηγῶν ἐπ᾽ ἐκκλησίαν ἐκάλει καὶ βουλὴν περὶ τοῦ πολέμου προὐτίθει, πυνθανόμενος δὲ εἰ χρὴ τὴν ἐπὶ Περσίδος ἐλαύνειν κἀκεῖσε τοῖς Τούρκοις συμπλέκεσθαι, ἢ μένοντα ἐπὶ τῆς ἰδίας τὴν ἐκείνων ἔλευσιν ἀναμένειν· ἠγγέλλετο γὰρ ἤδη καὶ ὁ σουλτάνος ἐξελθεῖν τῆς Περσίδος καὶ σχολῇ καὶ βάδην κατὰ Ῥωμαίων χωρεῖν. τοῖς μὲν οὖν ἐδόκει ὅσοι θρασύτερόν πως διέκειντο καὶ κολακικώτερον, μὴ μένειν, ἀλλ᾽ ἀπιέναι καὶ συμπλέκεσθαι τῷ σουλτάνῳ εἰσιόντι ἐν Βατάνοις τῆς Μηδίας. τῷ μαγίστρῳ δὲ Ἰωσὴφ τῷ Τραχανειώτῃ κατάρχοντι τότε ταγμάτων πολλῶν, καὶ τῷ δουκὶ πάσης δύσεως Νικηφόρῳ τῷ Βρυεννίῳ παντάπασιν ἐδόκει τὰ τοιαῦτα βουλεύματα σφάλλεσθαι, καὶ ἐξελιπάρουν τὸν βασιλέα, εἰ οἷόν τε εἴη, προσμένειν καὶ τοὺς πολεμίους ἕλκειν πρὸς ἑαυτὸν τὰς πέριξ πόλεις κατοχυρώσαντα καὶ τὰς πεδιάδας ἐμπρήσαντα, ὥστε σπανίζειν τοῖς πολεμίοις τὰ ἐπιτήδεια· εἰ δὲ μὴ τοῦτο, κἂν γοῦν καταλαβεῖν τὴν Θεοδοσίου πόλιν κἀκεῖσε στρατοπεδεύσαντα προσμένειν τοὺς πολεμίους, ὥστ᾽ ἀπορίᾳ τῶν ἀναγκαίων τὸν σουλτάνον ἀναγκασθῆναι τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις συμπλέκεσθαι ἔνθα Ῥωμαίους ξυμβαλεῖν πρὸς πόλεμον συμφέρον ἐστίν. ἀλλ᾽ ἐδόκουν παρὰ κωφῷ ᾄδειν, καὶ τὰ τῶν κολάκων ἐνίκα. καὶ δέον ἀνδράσι τὴν οἰκείαν ἀρετὴν παραστήσασιν ὑπακούειν, ὁ δὲ τοῖς κόλαξι μᾶλλον προσεῖχεν ἢ τοῖς ὀρθὰ συμβουλεύουσιν, ἐπηρμένος τοῖς προλαβοῦσι τροπαίοις καὶ μέγα ἐπὶ τούτοις φρονῶν. καὶ γὰρ τό τε Μέμπετ φρούριον εἷλε καὶ Τούρκων ἀποσπάσι προνομευόντων ἐντυχὼν ἐτρέψατό τε τούτους καὶ πολλοὺς μὲν ἀνεῖλεν, οὐκ ὀλίγους δὲ καὶ ἐζώγρησε. τούτοις οὖν ἐπαιρόμενος καὶ θαρρήσας πέρα τοῦ δέοντος ἅτε καὶ πλείονα τῶν προτέρων ἐπαγόμενος ξυμμαχίαν καὶ δύναμιν, ἄρας ξὺν παντὶ τῷ στρατεύματι τὴν εὐθὺ Περσίδος ἤλαυνε καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἐναντίους ἐχώρει.
units.en: 13. When he reached Cappadocia, he called the best of his generals to an assembly and put the war to counsel, asking whether he should march into Persia and engage the Turks there, or stay in his own land and wait for their coming; for it was already reported that the sultan had left Persia and was moving slowly, step by step, against the Romans. Those of a bolder and more flattering disposition thought he should not wait, but go out and engage the sultan as he entered Batana in Media. But to the magistros Joseph Trachaneiotes, then commanding many units, and to the doux of the whole West, Nikephoros Bryennios, such counsels seemed altogether mistaken, and they begged the emperor, if it were possible, to stay where he was and draw the enemy towards him, having fortified the towns around and burned the plains, so that the enemy should run short of supplies; or if not that, at least to occupy Theodosiopolis, camp there and wait for the enemy, so that for want of necessities the sultan should be forced to engage the Romans where it was to the Romans' advantage to fight. But they seemed to be singing to the deaf, and the flatterers' view prevailed. When he ought to have listened to men who had shown their own valour, he paid more attention to the flatterers than to those who gave him right advice, elated by his earlier trophies and proud of them. For he had taken the fort of Mempet, and, falling on detachments of Turks out foraging, had routed them, killing many and taking not a few alive. Elated by this, and more confident than he should have been, since he was bringing more allies and forces than before, he set out with the whole army on the road straight to Persia and advanced against the enemy.
units.note: The author's grandfather, the elder Nikephoros Bryennios, appears here among the wise counsellors who advised waiting at Theodosiopolis; Attaleiates has him sent out to skirmish and asking for help (Att. Battle [1]). Batana (Ecbatana, Hamadhan) is where Ibn al-Athīr says the sultan sent his baggage (IA Battle [2]).

units.orig: 14. Γενομένῳ δὲ τούτῳ περὶ τὸ Μαζίκερτον ὁ Βασιλάκιος ὑπηντίαζε στρατὸν ἐπαγόμενος οὐκ ὀλίγον ἐκ Συρίας καὶ Ἀρμενίας, ὃς ῥωμαλέος μὲν ὢν καὶ τὴν χεῖρα γενναῖος θρασὺς δὲ ἄλλως καὶ δυσκάθεκτος ταῖς ὁρμαῖς, καὶ τὸν βασιλέα κολακεύειν βουλόμενος, οὐδὲν ὑγιὲς ἐρωτώμενος ἀπεφθέγξατο. τοῦ γὰρ βεστάρχου Λέοντος τοῦ Διαβατηνοῦ γράμματα τῷ βασιλεῖ πεπομφότος, ὡς ὁ σουλτάνος φησὶ τὴν ἐκστρατείαν πυθόμενος καὶ δείσας τὴν δύναμιν, τὴν Περσίδα καταλιπὼν ἄπεισι φεύγων εἰς Βαβυλῶνα, τούτοις ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῖς λόγοις ἀναπεισθείς, διχῆ τὸ στράτευμα διελὼν τὴν μὲν τῶν δυνάμεων αὐτόθι κατεῖχε, τὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸ Χλέατ ἐξαποστέλλει, στρατηγὸν ἐπιστήσας αὐτοῖς τὸν μέγιστον Ἰωσὴφ τὸν Τραχανειώτην, ἄνδρα δεινὸν ἐν στρατιωτικοῖς βουλεύμασί τε καὶ στρατηγήμασιν, ἀπρόθυμον δὲ τότε παντάπασιν ὄντα καὶ τῷ βασιλεῖ παραινοῦντα εἴσω τὰς δυνάμεις ἁπάσας κατέχειν καὶ μὴ μερίζειν τὸ στράτευμα, ἀγχοῦ τῶν ἐναντίων στρατοπεδευόντων. ὃς ὡς ταῦτα λέγων οὐκ ἔπειθε, τὰς δυνάμεις ἀναλαβὼν πρὸς τὸ Χλέατ ἠπείγετο.
units.en: 14. When he was near Manzikert, Basilakios met him, bringing a considerable army from Syria and Armenia: a strong man, brave with his hand, but rash besides and hard to restrain in his impulses; and wishing to flatter the emperor, he said nothing sound when he was questioned. For the vestarches Leo Diabatenos had sent letters to the emperor saying that the sultan, on hearing of the campaign and fearing his forces, was leaving Persia and fleeing to Babylon; and the emperor, persuaded by these words, divided the army in two: part of the forces he kept there, and the other he sent off to Khliat, putting in command of them the megistos Joseph Trachaneiotes, a man formidable in military counsel and stratagem, but then wholly unwilling, who advised the emperor to keep all the forces inside and not to divide the army with the enemy camped nearby. When he did not persuade him by saying this, he took the forces and hurried to Khliat.
units.note: A reason for the division that the others do not give: a false report that the sultan was fleeing to Babylon (Baghdad). Trachaneiotes, who in Attaleiates fled ignobly with the detached army (Att. Battle [7]), is here a wise general sent away against his advice. Compare Att. March [4], Matt. Battle [3], Psell. Reign [11].

units.titel: 14. Basilakes rides out and is taken
units.orig: πόλις δὲ τὸ Χλέατ ὑπὸ τοὺς Τούρκους τελοῦσα, καὶ φρουρὰν ἔχον ἀποχρῶσαν ἔνδοθεν Τούρκων. ἀλλ᾽ οὔπω τρίτης διελθούσης ἡμέρας τοῖς ἐπὶ χόρτου συλλογὴν ἐξιοῦσιν ἐπιτίθενται Τοῦρκοι καὶ τινὰς μὲν ἀναιροῦσιν ἐνίους δὲ καὶ ζωγροῦσι. τοῦ ξυμβάντος γοῦν ἀπαγγελθέντος τῷ βασιλεῖ εὐθὺς ὁ Βασιλάκης μετεκέκλητο καὶ περὶ τῶν Τούρκων ἐπολυπραγμονεῖτο, τίνες τε εἶεν οἱ τὰς ἐπιθέσεις ποιούμενοι καὶ ὅθεν γῆς ἥκοντες. ὁ δὲ τῇ συνήθει θρασύτητι καὶ πάλιν χρησάμενος τοὺς ἐκ τοῦ Χλέατ ἥκειν ἐφ᾽ ἁρπαγῇ διενίστατο. ἔλαθεν οὖν οὕτω τὸν βασιλέα ἡ τοῦ σουλτάνου ἔφοδος οὐ μακρὰν τοῦ στρατοπέδου ὄντος καὶ τὰ τοῦ πολέμου εὖ διατιθεμένου. βουλόμενος γὰρ τὸν βασιλέα ἐπαγαγεῖν εἰς τὰ ἔμπροσθεν καὶ ἐντὸς ἀρκύων ποιήσασθαι, προδρόμους ἐξέπεμπεν, οἳ προέτρεχόν τε τοῖς ἵπποις περὶ τὸν τῶν Ῥωμαίων χάρακα, καὶ αὖθις ἀνθυπενόστουν ὥσπερ δρασμὸν ποιούμενοι. καὶ τοῦτο πολλάκις ποιοῦντες ἐνίους τῶν στρατηγῶν συνηρπάκασιν, ὧν ὁ πρῶτος ὁ Βασιλάκης ἦν. σπεύδων γὰρ οὗτος τὸν βασιλέα πληροφορῆσαι ὡς οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ Περσικοῦ στρατεύματος εἶεν οἱ τὰς ἐκδρομὰς ποιούμενοι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῶν ἐνοικούντων τῷ Χλέατ, ᾔτει συγχωρηθῆναί οἱ τοῦ χάρακος ἐξελθεῖν, καὶ τὸν ἀκινάκην σπασάμενος καὶ μυωπίσας τὸν ἵππον ἀσυντάκτως ἐχώρει κατὰ τῶν πολεμίων. καὶ οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν εἵποντο οὐ κατὰ τάξιν ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ ἔτυχεν ἕκαστος. ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ἄτακτον τούτων φορὰν οἱ πολέμιοι θεασάμενοι προσεποιήσαντο φεύγειν. ἐπεὶ δὲ πόρρω τοῦ χάρακος εἶδον αὐτοὺς ἐξελάσαντας, τοὺς χαλινοὺς ὑποστρέψαντες καὶ διεσκεδασμένοις αὐτοῖς προσβαλόντες νικῶσιν αὐτοὺς κατὰ κράτος. καὶ πίπτουσι μὲν πολλοὶ τῶν στρατιωτῶν, ὡς μικροῦ δεῖν μηδ᾽ ἄγγελον ὃ δὴ λέγεται διασωθῆναι τῆς συμφορᾶς, ἑάλω δὲ καὶ ὁ Βασιλάκης.
units.en: Khliat is a city subject to the Turks, with a sufficient garrison of Turks inside. But before the third day had passed, Turks fell on those who went out to gather fodder, killing some and taking others alive. When this was reported to the emperor, Basilakes was at once summoned and questioned about the Turks: who they were who were making these attacks, and from what land they came. He, again with his usual rashness, insisted that they were men from Khliat come for plunder. So the sultan's approach escaped the emperor, though he was not far from the camp and had disposed his war well. Wishing to lead the emperor on and get him inside his nets, he sent out skirmishers, who ran forward on their horses round the Roman palisade and turned back again as if in flight. And doing this many times they caught some of the generals, of whom Basilakes was the first. For in his haste to convince the emperor that those making the raids were not from the Persian army but from the inhabitants of Khliat, he asked to be allowed to leave the palisade, drew his sword, spurred his horse and charged the enemy in no order; and those with him followed not in rank but each as it happened. The enemy, seeing their disorderly rush, pretended to flee; and when they saw them ridden far from the palisade, they turned their reins, fell on them scattered, and beat them by force. Many of the soldiers fell, so that hardly even a messenger, as they say, escaped the disaster; and Basilakes was taken.
units.note: Several sentences are Psellos' almost word for word ('to lead him on and get him inside his nets … as if in flight … caught some of the generals', Psell. Reign [10]): the younger Bryennios used the Chronographia. The capture of Basilakes is Att. Battle [3]; in Attaleiates the elder Bryennios holds back his men while Basilakes charges.

units.titel: 15. The author's grandfather goes out, and is wounded
units.orig: 15. Ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἀπηγγέλη τῷ βασιλεῖ ὡς ὁ Βασιλάκης ἀσυντάκτως τοῦ χάρακος ἐξελθὼν κατὰ τῶν πολεμίων ἐλαύνει, τὸν δοῦκα πάσης δύσεως μετακαλεσάμενος τὸν Βρυέννιον τοῦ ἀριστεροῦ τηνικαῦτα κατάρχοντα κέρατος, ἐκπέμπει τοῦτον μετὰ τῆς οἰκείας δυνάμεως ἀπιέναι τὴν ταχίστην κελεύσας, ὡς εἴ τι δεινὸν ἐπισυμβαίη τῷ Βασιλάκῃ ἐπαμύνηται τούτῳ καὶ τῆς ἐκτροπῆς ἐπαμύνηται· ἤδη γὰρ ἐν αἰσθήσει γενέσθαι ἤρξατο τοῦ κακοῦ. ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀπῄει καὶ τὰς δυνάμεις ἐξῆγε τοῦ χάρακος ἐξιών. οὐδένα οὖν ἑώρα φίλων ἢ πολεμίων σπεύδων ἐπὶ τὰ πρόσω παραχωροῦντα, ἤρξατο δὲ ὁρᾶν περὶ γηλόφους πολεμίους συνεστηκότας, βραχὺ δὲ προϊὼν καὶ νεκροῖς ἐνέτυχε σώμασι καὶ ἠπόρει τί ποτ᾽ ἂν ὁ Βασιλάκης γέγονεν. ἐντυχὼν δὲ στρατιώτῃ ἔτι ἐμπνέοντι ἐπυνθάνετο ποῦ ποτ᾽ ἂν εἴη ὁ Βασιλάκης, καὶ τί τὸ περὶ αὐτοὺς ὁρώμενον. ὁ μὲν ἀπήγγελλε σύμπαντα, οἱ Τοῦρκοι δὲ πανταχόθεν συνέθεον καὶ κυκλοῦν ἐπειρῶντο τὴν φάλαγγα. αἰσθόμενος τοῦτο ὁ δοὺξ παρεκάλει τοὺς στρατιώτας ἄνδρας ἀγαθοὺς ὀφθῆναι, καὶ μηδέν τι δρᾶσαι τῶν ἀγεννῶν καὶ τῆς Ῥωμαϊκῆς ἀνάξιον γενναιότητος. στρέψας οὖν τὴν φάλαγγα ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ στρατόπεδον συντεταγμένως ἐχώρει, τῶν ἐπιόντων μηδένα λόγον ποιούμενος. ὡς δ᾽ ἔγγιστα τοῦ χάρακος γέγονε, μέρος ἀναλαβὼν τῆς φάλαγγος καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους προσμένειν κελεύσας ἐξαίφνης κατὰ τῶν ἐπιόντων ἐπήλασε καὶ ῥᾳδίως τούτους ἐτρέψατο. ἐπεὶ δὲ τοὺς λοιποὺς ἑώρα συνθέοντας παμπληθεί, πάντας ἀναλαβὼν ὑπέστρεψε πρὸς τὴν φάλαγγα. ἐπιθεμένων δ᾽ αὐτῷ τῶν Τούρκων καὶ κυκλωσάντων, δόρατι μὲν ἐτρώθη κατὰ τῶν στέρνων, βέλεσι δὲ δυσὶ κατὰ τῶν μεταφρένων. ἡρωϊκῶς δ᾽ ἀγωνισάμενος πρὸς τὴν φάλαγγα διασέσωστο καὶ ξὺν αὐτῇ κατέλαβε τὸ στρατόπεδον. ἀπελθὼν δὲ πρὸς βασιλέα καὶ τὰ ξυμβάντα διηγησάμενος ἐκελεύσθη πρὸς τῇ σκηνῇ γενέσθαι καὶ θεραπεύειν τὰ τραύματα.
units.en: 15. When it was reported to the emperor that Basilakes had left the palisade in disorder and was riding against the enemy, he summoned the doux of the whole West, Bryennios, who was then commanding the left wing, and sent him out with his own forces, ordering him to go as quickly as possible, so that if anything terrible should befall Basilakes he might help him and cover his retreat; for he had already begun to sense the danger. So he went, and led his forces out of the palisade. Hurrying forward he saw no one, friend or foe, …; but then he began to see enemies gathered on the hillocks, and going on a little he came upon dead bodies and was at a loss what had become of Basilakes. Coming on a soldier still breathing, he asked where Basilakes might be and what it was they were looking at. He told him everything; and the Turks were running together from every side and trying to encircle the line. Seeing this, the doux urged the soldiers to show themselves brave men and to do nothing base or unworthy of Roman nobility. So he turned the line and went towards the camp in order, taking no account of the attackers. When he was very near the palisade, he took part of the line, told the others to wait, suddenly charged the attackers and easily routed them. But when he saw the rest running together in full force, he took them all and returned to the line. As the Turks attacked and surrounded him, he was wounded by a spear in the chest and by two arrows in the back. Having fought heroically he got safely back to the line and with it reached the camp. He went to the emperor, told what had happened, and was ordered to stay by his tent and look after his wounds.
units.note: The author's grandfather as hero. Attaleiates has the same Bryennios hold back his men so that Basilakes pursued alone (Att. Battle [3]), and ask for more troops out of fear (Att. Battle [1]). Meineke thinks the sentence 'he saw no one … παραχωροῦντα' is corrupt; the word is left untranslated.

units.titel: 16. The worse counsel again; the order of battle
units.orig: 16. Καὶ τότε μὲν ἔμεινε παρὰ τῇ σκηνῇ· ἡμέρας δ᾽ ἤδη διαγελώσης καὶ τοῦ ἡλίου ὁρίζοντα ὑπερβαίνοντος αὖθις μετεκαλεῖτο παρὰ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος. ὁ δ᾽ ἀπῄει τῶν τραυμάτων καταφρονήσας. ὡς δὲ βουλὴ προετέθη ἢ πολεμεῖν ἢ εἴσω τὰς δυνάμεις κατέχειν, τοῖς μὲν ἐδόκει συνετῶς ἄγαν εἴσω μένειν τοῦ χάρακος καὶ τὰς δυνάμεις ἐκ τοῦ Χλέατ μεταπέμπεσθαι, τοῖς δὲ κόλαξι τἀναντία, εἰ μὲν καὶ οὕτω φρονοῦσιν, οὐκ ἔχω λέγειν. τέως δ᾽ ἔδοξε, καὶ αὖθις ἐνίκα τὰ χερείονα. ἐξάγειν οὖν τὰς δυνάμεις ἐγένετο. οἱ δέ γε Τοῦρκοι κραταιότεροι αὖθις καὶ μετὰ πλείονος ἐπήρχοντο τῆς χειρός. καὶ δὴ προσβάλλουσι τούτῳ, καὶ μάχης συστάσης πίπτουσι μὲν τῶν Τούρκων συχνοί, πίπτουσι δὲ καὶ τῶν Ῥωμαίων πλεῖστοι. ἐτρώθη δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Βρυέννιος πολλαχοῦ τοῦ σώματος, ἀλλὰ δεινὸς ὢν περὶ τὰ στρατηγικὰ τὸ πλεῖστον τῆς φάλαγγος ἀσινὲς διεσώσατο. ὁρῶν δ᾽ ἐπιόντας τοὺς Τούρκους ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐξῆγε καὶ αὐτὸς τὰς δυνάμεις ὡς ἐπὶ πόλεμον καὶ παρετάττετο πρὸ τοῦ χάρακος. ἡγεῖτο δὲ τοῦ μὲν δεξιοῦ κέρατος ὁ Ἀλυάττης, ἀνὴρ Καππαδόκης καὶ συνήθης τῷ βασιλεῖ, τοῦ δ᾽ εὐωνύμου αὐτὸς ὁ Βρυέννιος, τὸ δὲ μέσον τῆς φάλαγγος εἶχεν ὁ βασιλεύς. οὐραγεῖν δὲ ἐτέτακτο ὁ τοῦ καίσαρος υἱὸς ὁ πρόεδρος Ἀνδρόνικος τάς τε τῶν ἑταίρων τάξεις ἔχων καὶ τὰς τῶν ἀρχόντων, ἀνὴρ καὶ γένους λαμπροῦ καὶ πᾶσι κομῶν τοῖς καλοῖς· φρονήσει γὰρ τῶν ἡλίκων ἁπάντων ὑπέρτερος, καὶ ἀνδρικώτατος εἴπερ τις ἄλλος, καὶ ταῖς στρατηγικαῖς ἐντραφεὶς μελέταις, οὐ πάνυ δὲ φιλίως ἔχων πρὸς βασιλέα.
units.en: 16. Then he stayed by the tent; but when day was already smiling and the sun was rising above the horizon, he was summoned again by the emperor, and went, disregarding his wounds. When the question was put whether to fight or to keep the forces inside, some thought, very wisely, that they should stay inside the palisade and send for the forces from Khliat; the flatterers thought the opposite (whether they really thought so, I cannot say). Meanwhile it was decided, and again the worse prevailed. So the forces were led out. The Turks came on again stronger and in greater numbers. They attacked him, and in the battle that followed many of the Turks fell, and very many of the Romans too. Bryennios himself was wounded in many places on his body, but being formidable in generalship he brought most of his line through unharmed. Seeing the Turks coming on, the emperor too led out the forces as for battle and drew them up before the palisade. The right wing was led by Alyates, a Cappadocian and an intimate of the emperor; the left by Bryennios himself; the centre of the line the emperor held. The rearguard was assigned to the Caesar's son, the proedros Andronikos, who had the companies of the Companions and of the lords: a man of brilliant family and flourishing in every good quality, for in intelligence he surpassed all of his age, was as manly as anyone, and was brought up in the exercises of generalship; but he was not at all friendly disposed towards the emperor.
units.note: Meineke's apparatus: 'wounds' is Possinus' correction for 'armies'. The order of battle is Bryennios' alone: Alyates on the right (the Cappadocian later blinded in the civil war, Att. Civil [1]), the author's grandfather on the left, Andronikos in the rear with the aristocratic companies, praised in every way, and 'not at all friendly disposed towards the emperor'. The author was writing for Andronikos' daughter Eirene Doukaina.

units.titel: 17. The battle: the right breaks, the rear withdraws
units.orig: 17. Οἱ δὲ Τοῦρκοι τὸν βασιλέα βλέποντες παρατάττοντα τὸν στρατὸν οὐ κατὰ φάλαγγας οὐδὲ κατὰ λόχους (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐβούλοντο Ῥωμαίοις εἰς χεῖρας ἐλθεῖν) ἡσύχασαν. ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν σουλτάνος πόρρω που ἱστάμενος τὰ πρὸς πόλεμον διετάττετο, ἀνδρὶ δέ τινι ἐκτομίᾳ τὰ μέγιστα παρ᾽ αὐτῷ δυναμένῳ, Ταράγγης τούτῳ τὸ ὄνομα, τὰς πλείστας δυνάμεις παραδοὺς κύριον τοῦ πολέμου τοῦτον ἀπέδειξεν. ὁ δὲ εἰς πολλὰ μέρη τὸ στράτευμα διελὼν προλοχισμούς τε ἐποίει καὶ ἐνέδρας συνίστα, καὶ περιιέναι τὰς τάξεις Ῥωμαίων ἐπέταττε καὶ τοῖς τοξεύμασι χρῆσθαι πάντοθεν. οἱ δὲ Ῥωμαῖοι τῶν ἵππων αὐτῶν βαλλομένων ἠναγκάζοντο ἕπεσθαι. καὶ δὴ εἵποντο φεύγειν δοκούντων ἐκείνων. εἰς δὲ τοὺς λόχους καὶ τὰς ἐνέδρας περιπίπτοντες μεγάλως ἐβλάπτοντο. τοῦ βασιλέως δὲ τὸν ὑπὲρ τῶν ὅλων βουλομένου κίνδυνον ἀναδέξασθαι βάδην ἑπομένου καὶ προσδοκῶντος φάλαγγα Τούρκων εὑρεῖν καὶ αὐτῇ συρραγῆναι καὶ οὕτω κριθῆναι τὰ τοῦ πολέμου, οἱ Τοῦρκοι πανταχόθεν διεσκεδάννυντο. ὑποστρέψαντες δὲ μετὰ ῥύμης σφοδρᾶς καὶ κραυγῆς ἐπελθόντες Ῥωμαίοις τρέπουσι τὸ δεξιὸν κέρας. εὐθὺς δ᾽ ἀνεχώρουν καὶ οἱ περὶ τὴν οὐραγίαν, καὶ τὸν βασιλέα οἱ Τοῦρκοι κυκλώσαντες ἔβαλλον πάντοθεν. ὁρμήσαντος δὲ τοῦ εὐωνύμου κέρατος ἐπαρήγειν οἱ Τοῦρκοι ἐκώλυον· κατὰ νώτου γὰρ οὗτοι γενόμενοι καὶ τοῦτον κυκλώσαντες φυγεῖν κατηνάγκασαν. ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς παντάπασιν ἔρημος ἀποληφθεὶς βοηθείας τὸ ξίφος ἐγύμνωσεν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἐχθροὺς καὶ πολλοὺς μὲν ἀνεῖλε τοὺς δὲ καὶ φυγεῖν κατηνάγκασε. κυκλωθεὶς δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων τοῦ πλήθους τὴν χεῖρα τιτρώσκεται καὶ γνωσθεὶς ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν ὅστις ἐστὶ κύκλῳ περιστοιχίζεται πάντοθεν. καὶ τοξεύεται μὲν ὁ ἵππος αὐτοῦ καὶ ὀλισθήσας πίπτει, συγκαταβάλλει δὲ καὶ τὸν ἐπιβάτην. καὶ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον δορυάλωτος ὁ βασιλεὺς Ῥωμαίων γίνεται καὶ πρὸς τὸν σουλτάνον ἀποκομίζεται δέσμιος, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ οἷστισι λόγοις τοῦτο τῆς θείας προνοίας οἰκονομησάσης.
units.en: 17. The Turks, seeing the emperor draw up his army, did not stay still in battle lines or companies (for they did not want to come to close quarters with the Romans). The sultan stood somewhere far off arranging the battle, and gave most of his forces to a eunuch who had the greatest power with him, Taranges by name, and made him master of the battle. He divided the army into many parts, set ambushes and traps, and ordered them to go round the Roman ranks and shoot arrows from every side. The Romans, with their horses being shot, were forced to follow; and they followed, the enemy seeming to flee; and falling into the ambushes and traps they were greatly harmed. While the emperor, wishing to take on the danger for the whole, followed step by step, expecting to find a line of Turks, clash with it and so decide the battle, the Turks scattered in every direction. Then, turning back with a violent rush and a shout, they fell on the Romans and routed the right wing. At once those of the rearguard withdrew too, and the Turks surrounded the emperor and shot at him from every side. When the left wing moved to help, the Turks prevented it: they got behind it, surrounded it, and forced it to flee. The emperor, cut off entirely alone without help, bared his sword against the enemy, killed many and forced others to flee. Surrounded by the mass of the enemy he was wounded in the hand, and being recognised by them for who he was, he was ringed round on every side. His horse was shot, slipped and fell, and threw its rider down with it. In this way the emperor of the Romans became a prisoner of war and was carried to the sultan in chains, by what reasons divine providence arranged this I do not know.
units.note: Bryennios alone names the Turkish commander, the eunuch Taranges. 'At once those of the rearguard withdrew too': the Doukas rearguard withdraws in the same sentence as the right wing breaks, without a rumour and without treachery; compare Att. Battle [12], where 'most people assert' a cousin of the emperor's stepson spread the rumour, and Matt. Battle [5], where the Uzes and Pechenegs go over. The last sentences follow Psellos (Psell. Battle [2]).

units.titel: 17. The camp, the regalia, and the pearl called the Orphan
units.orig: ἑάλω δὲ καὶ λοιπῶν μοῖρα τῶν ἀρχόντων οὐκ ὀλίγη. τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν οἱ μὲν μαχαίρας ἔργον γεγόνασιν, οἱ δὲ διεσώθησαν. ἑάλω δὲ καὶ τό τε στρατόπεδον ἅπαν καὶ ἡ σκηνὴ ἡ βασίλειος καὶ τὰ χρήματα καὶ τῶν βασιλικῶν παρασήμων τὰ κάλλιστα, ἐν οἷς καὶ ὁ πολυθρύλλητος μάργαρος ἦν, ὃν ὀρφανὸν κατωνόμαζον. οἱ δ᾽ ἐκ τῆς μάχης διασωθέντες ἄλλος ἀλλαχοῦ διεσπάρησαν, τὴν ἰδίαν ἕκαστος καταλαβεῖν σπεύδοντες.
units.en: No small part of the rest of the lords was taken too. Of the others, some became the work of the sword and some escaped. The whole camp was taken, and the imperial tent, and the money, and the finest of the imperial insignia, among them the famous pearl they called the Orphan. Those who escaped from the battle scattered, each hurrying to reach his own land.
units.note: Meineke would delete λοιπῶν. The Orphan was a great single pearl of the imperial regalia; its loss is reported only here.

sections.titel: The coup and the persecution of the Komnenoi (1071)
sections.blurb: Messengers in the City, the Caesar summoned from his hunting in Bithynia, terms 'not unworthy of the Romans', the Caesar's sons and the axe-bearers proclaiming Michael, the empress in a crypt with the guards shouting at its mouth, Amaseia and Khatchatour, and the trial of Anna Dalassene, mother of the Komnenoi, who brings out an icon of Christ as her judge.

units.titel: 18. Messengers; the Caesar summoned from Bithynia
units.orig: 18. Οὐ πολλαὶ δ᾽ ἡμέραι διεληλύθεσαν, καὶ τῶν διαδράντων τὸν πόλεμον ἄγγελός τις προλαβὼν τὸ δεινὸν ἐν τῇ πόλει ἀπήγγειλε, καὶ αὖθις ἄλλος καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις τρίτος καὶ τέταρτος, σαφὲς μὲν οὐδὲν ἀπαγγέλλειν ἔχοντες, αὐτὸ δὲ μόνον τὸ δεινὸν ἐξηγούμενοι καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλως διερμηνεύοντες· οἱ μὲν γὰρ αὐτὸν τὸν βασιλέα τεθνηκέναι κατήγγελλον, οἱ δὲ ἑαλωκέναι, οἱ δὲ τετρωμένον τοῦτον ἰδεῖν καὶ κατὰ γῆς ἐρριμμένον, οἱ δὲ δέσμιον ἀπαγόμενον εἰς τὸ τῶν ἐναντίων στρατόπεδον. ἐπὶ συμβούλοις οὖν τῇ βασιλίδι τὰ πράγματα, καὶ ὁ καῖσαρ εὐθὺς μετεκέκλητο περὶ Βιθυνίαν διάγων καὶ σχολάζων κυνηγεσίοις διὰ τὸ ὕποπτον εἶναι τῷ βασιλεῖ. μήπω δὲ τούτου καταλαβόντος ἡ βασιλὶς διηρώτα τί ποτε ἄρα χρὴ πράττειν. ἔδοξεν οὖν πᾶσιν ἐκεῖνον μὲν τέως ἐᾶσαι εἴτε ἑάλω εἴτε τέθνηκεν, ἑαυτῇ δὲ καὶ τοῖς παισὶ κρατύνεσθαι τὴν ἀρχήν. ἔτι δὲ μετεώρου ὄντος τοῦ πράγματος γίνεται κοινωνὸς ὁ καῖσαρ. ὁ δὲ τήν τε κοινοπραγίαν ἀσπάζεται, καὶ συμπράττειν ἀμφότερα ὅσα τῇ βασιλείᾳ προσήκει πράγματα τήν τε μητέρα καὶ τὸν πρεσβύτερον τῶν υἱῶν ἀποφαίνεται, τὸν μὲν ὡς τεκοῦσαν σεβάζεσθαι, τὴν δὲ κοινῇ μετὰ τοῦ παιδὸς τὴν τῶν ὅλων ποιεῖσθαι οἰκονομίαν. οὕτω μὲν καὶ τῷ βασιλεῖ Μιχαὴλ ἐδόκει, καὶ ξυνετίθετο τῷ τοῦ θείου σκοπῷ. ἀλλ᾽ οἱ τῶν κοινῶν κατατρυφᾶν πραγμάτων βουλόμενοι καὶ κέρδους ἕνεκα τοῦ σφετέρου τὰ περὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν πραγματεύεσθαι, τὴν μὲν εἰς μοναρχίαν ἠρέθιζον, τὸν δ᾽ ὁπλίζειν ἔσπευδον κατὰ τῆς μητρός.
units.en: 18. Not many days had passed when a messenger from those who had run from the war got ahead and reported the disaster in the City, and then another, and after them a third and a fourth, with nothing clear to report, only explaining the disaster itself, each interpreting it his own way: some announced that the emperor himself was dead, others that he was taken, others that they had seen him wounded and thrown to the ground, others led away in chains to the enemy camp. So the affairs of the empress came to counsel, and the Caesar was at once summoned: he was living in Bithynia, passing his time in hunting, because he was suspect to the emperor. Before he arrived the empress asked what should be done. It seemed good to all to leave him aside for the time being, whether he was taken or dead, and that she and her sons should secure the government. While the matter was still undecided, the Caesar became a partner in it. He embraced the joint rule, and declared that both, the mother and the eldest of the sons, should share in all the business of the empire, he honouring her as his mother, she managing the whole of affairs jointly with her son. So it seemed right to the emperor Michael too, and he agreed with his uncle's aim. But those who wanted to feast on public affairs and handle the government for their own gain stirred her up to rule alone and hurried to arm him against his mother.
units.note: Taken almost word for word from Psellos (Psell. Battle [3], [5]), with one detail of the family's own: the Caesar in Bithynia, hunting, 'because he was suspect to the emperor'.

units.titel: 19. Terms not unworthy of the Romans; the letter
units.orig: 19. Ἀλλ᾽ οὔπω τούτου κατευνασθέντος τοῦ κύματος ἕτερον ἠγείρετο καὶ ἐπωρύετο. ὁ γὰρ Περσῶν ἀρχηγὸς ἐπειδὴ τὸν βασιλέα Ῥωμαίων δορυάλωτον ἐθεάσατο οὐκ ἐπήρθη τῷ κατορθώματι, συνεστάλη δὲ μᾶλλον τῷ εὐτυχήματι καὶ μετριάζει τῇ νίκῃ τοσοῦτον ὅσον οὐδεὶς ἐνενόησε. παραμυθεῖται τὸν ἑαλωκότα, κοινωνεῖ τραπέζης, λύει αὐτῷ τῶν δεσμωτῶν οὓς ἐβούλετο, τελευταῖον καὶ αὐτὸν τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας ἐλευθεροῖ. καὶ σύμβολα κήδους πεποιηκὼς καὶ ὑποσχέσεις παρ᾽ ἐκείνου λαβὼν ἐνωμότους οὐκ ἀναξίας Ῥωμαίων (ἐβούλετο γὰρ ὁ βασιλεὺς μᾶλλον τεθνάναι ἢ ἀναξίας συμβιβάσεις ποιεῖσθαι τῆς ἑαυτοῦ γενναιότητος), αὖθις ἐπὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ἐκπέμπει ἀρχὴν μεθ᾽ ὅσης ἂν εἴποι τις προπομπῆς καὶ δορυφορίας. ὅπερ δὴ ἀρχέκακον ἐγεγόνει καὶ πολλῶν συμφορῶν αἰτιώτατον. τυχὼν γὰρ ὁ βασιλεὺς παραδόξως ὧνπερ οὐκ ἤλπιζεν, ἀπραγματεύτως ᾠήθη τὴν βασιλείαν Ῥωμαίων λήψεσθαι αὖθις, καὶ ὥσπερ αὐτάγγελος τοῦ μετὰ τοῦτο μέγιστον ἐκείνου ἀτύχημα εὐτυχήματος τῇ βασιλίδι καθίστατο, γράμμασι τῆς ἰδίας χειρὸς ἃ συμβεβήκει τούτῳ σημειωσάμενος. θόρυβος οὖν καὶ συνδρομὴ εὐθὺς περὶ τὰ βασίλεια, τῶν μὲν θαυμαζόντων τὸ γεγονός, τῶν δὲ ἀπιστούντων τῷ πράγματι. μετέωρος δὲ ἦν καὶ ἡ βασιλὶς σκεπτομένη τί ποτ᾽ ἂν δράσειε, καὶ τὸ περὶ αὐτὴν εὔνουν συγκαλουμένη παρεσκεύαζε σκέμματα.
units.en: 19. But before this wave had been laid to rest, another rose and roared. The chief of the Persians, when he saw the emperor of the Romans a prisoner of war, was not elated by his success but rather humbled by his good fortune, and was as moderate in victory as no one had imagined. He consoled the captive, shared his table, released to him those prisoners he wished, and finally set him too free from captivity; and having made tokens of a marriage alliance and received sworn promises from him not unworthy of the Romans (for the emperor would rather have died than make terms unworthy of his own nobility), he sent him back to his own empire with all the escort and guard one could describe. This was the beginning of evils and the chief cause of many misfortunes. For the emperor, having unexpectedly got what he had not hoped for, thought he would take back the empire of the Romans without trouble, and, as if bringing the news himself of the good fortune that followed that greatest misfortune, he wrote to the empress in his own hand what had happened to him. At once there was uproar and running together in the palace, some marvelling at what had happened, others disbelieving it. The empress too was in suspense, considering what she should do, and called together those loyal to her and prepared plans.
units.note: From Psellos (Psell. Battle [6]), with one addition of the family's: the terms were 'not unworthy of the Romans', for the emperor would rather have died. Ibn al-Athīr names the terms (IA Battle [9]).

units.titel: 20. The Caesar's sons, the axe-bearers, and the empress in a crypt
units.orig: 20. **** δείσας γὰρ περὶ ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τοῖν ἀδελφοπαίδοιν μὴ καὶ πάθοιεν δεινὸν τοῦ Διογένους αὖθις κατασχόντος τὴν βασιλείαν, τοὺς περὶ τὴν αὐλὴν φύλακας εὐθὺς οἰκειοῦται. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος ὥρμητο ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου χώρας τῆς πλησίον ὠκεανοῦ, πιστὸν δὲ βασιλεῦσι Ῥωμαίων ἀρχῆθεν, ἀσπιδηφόρον ξύμπαν καὶ πέλεκύν τινα ἐπὶ ὤμων φέρον. δίχα οὖν αὐτοὺς διελὼν τοῖς μὲν ἐκέλευσε τοῖς υἱέσιν ἕπεσθαι καὶ τὰ κελευσθέντα πληροῦν, τοῖς δὲ ξυνέπεσθαί οἱ καὶ ὁδηγῷ τούτῳ χρῆσθαι πρὸς τὴν μελετωμένην ἐγχείρησιν. ἀλλ᾽ οἱ μὲν περὶ τὸν κλεινὸν Ἀνδρόνικόν τε καὶ Κωνσταντῖνον (οὕτω γὰρ ὠνομάζοντο ἄμφω τὼ παῖδε τοῦ καίσαρος) περιστάντες τὸν βασιλέα καὶ χορὸν περὶ αὐτὸν ἑλίξαντες, ἀθρόον ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότερα τῶν ἀνακτόρων ἀνάγουσιν, ἡγουμένων τῶν παίδων τοῦ καίσαρος καὶ αὐτοκράτορα τὸν Μιχαὴλ ἀναγορευόντων. οἱ δὲ περὶ τὸν καίσαρα κτυπήσαντες τὰς ἀσπίδας ἀθρόοι καὶ βαρβαρικὸν ἀλαλάξαντες τάς τε ῥομφαίας πρὸς ἀλλήλων συντρίψαντές τε καὶ συγκροτήσαντες περὶ τὴν βασιλίδος ἐχώρουν σκηνήν. ἡ δὲ τοῦ θορύβου καὶ τῆς κραυγῆς αἰσθομένη οὐδὲ καθεκτὴ ἔτι ἦν, ἀλλὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς περιελομένη τὸ κάλυμμα ἐπί τι οἴκημα ἄδυτον ἐμφερὲς σπηλαίῳ ἐξώρμα. καὶ ἡ μὲν ἐδεδύκει τῷ φωλεῷ, οἱ δὲ περιειστήκεισαν τὸ στόμιον ἀλαλάζοντες καὶ φόβον μέγιστον αὐτῇ ἐπισείοντες. καὶ μικροῦ ἂν ἐτεθνήκει, εἰ μὴ ὁ καῖσαρ εἰσδὺς τὸ πολὺ τοῦ φόβου αὐτῇ διελύσατο. ξυνεβούλευε γοῦν ἀπιέναι τῶν ἀνακτόρων αὐτήν, μὴ καὶ πάθῃ τι τῶν ἀνηκέστων πρὸς τῶν φυλάκων. ἡ δὲ ἐπείθετό τε καὶ κατῄει ὡς ἐπὶ θάλασσαν, καὶ εἰς τὸν δρόμωνα τὸν βασιλικὸν εἰσελθοῦσα ἀπῄει ἔνθα οἰκεῖν κατακέκριτο, εἰς ὅπερ αὕτη δηλαδὴ τοῦ Στενοῦ πρὸς τῇ θαλάσσῃ τέμενος τῇ θεοτόκῳ ἱδρύσατο. οὔπω συχνὸς παρερρύη καιρός, καὶ δεύτερον κατ᾽ αὐτῆς δόγμα γίνεται εἰς τὴν μοναδικὴν αὐτὴν μετατεθῆναι ζωήν. καὶ αὐτίκα δὴ καὶ τοῦτο τετέλεστο. ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν κατὰ τὴν βασιλίδα εἰς τοῦτο συντέτακται.
units.en: 20. **** For fearing for himself and his two nephews, lest they suffer something terrible if Diogenes took the throne again, he at once won over the palace guards. This race came from the barbarian land near the Ocean and has been loyal to the emperors of the Romans from the beginning: all shield-bearers, carrying a kind of axe on their shoulders. He divided them in two and ordered some to follow his sons and carry out their orders, and the others to go with him and take him as their guide in the undertaking planned. Those with the famous Andronikos and Constantine (for so the Caesar's two sons were called) surrounded the emperor, formed a dance round him and took him all together to the upper parts of the palace, the Caesar's sons leading and proclaiming Michael autokrator. Those with the Caesar beat their shields all together, raised a barbarian war cry, clashed and rang their swords against each other, and went to the empress's quarters. She, hearing the uproar and the shouting, could no longer be held, but tore the covering from her head and rushed to an underground chamber like a cave. She crept into the hole, and they stood round its mouth, shouting and shaking the greatest fear upon her. She would all but have died had not the Caesar gone in and dispelled most of her fear. He advised her to leave the palace, lest she suffer something irreparable at the hands of the guards. She obeyed, went down to the sea, boarded the imperial dromon and went away to where she had been condemned to live, the precinct she herself had founded to the Mother of God by the sea at the Stenon. Not much time had passed when a second decree was made against her, that she should be changed over to the monastic life; and at once this too was done. So much for the empress.
units.note: The asterisks are the lacuna Possinus marked: the subject, the Caesar John, is lost with it. Bryennios gives the coup to the Caesar outright; Psellos makes Michael the actor and himself the man at the crypt's mouth (Psell. Coup [2], [3]). Here the Varangians shout at the mouth of the crypt and the Caesar comes in to reassure her. The guard's axes and its home 'near the Ocean' are Bryennios' additions.

units.orig: 21. Διογένης δ᾽ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας ἀπολυθεὶς δεινὸν ἡγεῖτο εἰ μὴ αὖθις τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐπιλάβοιτο. καὶ δὴ πέμπων εἰς τὰς ἁπανταχοῦ πόλεις καὶ χώρας στρατεύματά τε συνήθροιζε καὶ χρήματα εἰσεπράττετο. ἤδη δὲ πλήθους αὐτῷ συνερρυηκότος στρατηγικῆς φάλαγγος τὸ διὰ πάσης γλώττης βοώμενον πόλισμα, φημὶ δὲ τὴν Ἀμάσειαν, μετὰ παντὸς τοῦ στρατοπέδου καταλαμβάνει. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μαθόντες οἱ περὶ τὸν βασιλέα τε καὶ τὸν καίσαρα ἐσκόπουν τίνα τούτῳ ἀντίπαλον καταστήσειαν. ἔδοξεν οὖν τῶν τοῦ καίσαρος υἱέων τῷ νεωτέρῳ τὸ Ῥωμαϊκὸν πιστεύειν στρατόπεδον, ἀνδρὶ καὶ τὴν χεῖρα γενναίῳ καὶ τὴν σύνεσιν ὀξεῖ τε καὶ θαυμασίῳ. ὁ δὲ τὰς δυνάμεις λαβὼν ἐχώρει κατὰ τοῦ Διογένους, καὶ ἀγχοῦ κατὰ τῆς Ἀμασείας γενόμενος πρῶτα μὲν συνῆγε τὸ στράτευμα καὶ ἀκροβολισμοῖς ἐχρῆτο, καὶ πάντα τρόπον ἐμηχανᾶτο ἢ αἱρήσειν τὸν Διογένην ἢ ἐξελάσειν τῆς πόλεως. ὁ δὲ στενοχωρούντων τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῷ ἠναγκάσθη τὰς δυνάμεις ἐξαγαγεῖν καὶ παρατάττεσθαι πρὸς τὸν δοῦκα. μίγνυνται οὖν ἀμφότερα τὰ στρατόπεδα, καὶ πίπτουσιν ἑκατέρωθεν πλεῖστοι τῶν στρατηγῶν ἑκατέρων γενναίως ἀγωνιζομένων. φεύγουσι δ᾽ ὅμως οἱ περὶ τὸν Διογένην, τοῦ Δούκα Κωνσταντίνου γενναιότερον προσβαλόντος τοῖς κατὰ μέτωπον ἱσταμένοις καὶ τὴν ἐκείνων ὠθήσαντος φάλαγγα. πίπτουσιν οὖν πολλοὶ τῶν περὶ τὸν Διογένην, αὐτὸς δὲ διαφεύγει καὶ σὺν ὀλίγοις τοῖς περὶ αὐτὸν εἴς τι κλείεται φρούριον. τοῦτο πρῶτον θάρσους αἴτιον τοῖς περὶ τὸν βασιλέα Μιχαὴλ γίνεται, καὶ Διογένης ἐντεῦθεν ἀρχὴν λαμβάνει τῆς καταλύσεως. καὶ ἑάλω ἂν αὐτίκα, εἰ μή τι ἄλλο συνεπεπτώκει. ἀνὴρ γάρ τις ἐξ Ἀρμενίας τὸ γένος ἀνέλκων, τὴν γνώμην βαθύς, τὴν χεῖρα γενναῖος ὁ Κουτατάριος ἦν, ἀρχήν τινα παρὰ τοῦ Διογένους τῶν μεγίστων λαβών, ὁπηνίκα ἐκεῖνος βασιλεὺς Ῥωμαίων ἐχρημάτιζε, χάριτας αὐτῷ ἐπὶ τοῦ δυστυχήματος ἀνθομολογούμενος, στρατιώτας συχνοὺς ἐπαγόμενος πρόσεισι τούτῳ καὶ θαρρεῖν παρακελευσάμενος καὶ τὰ μέγιστα ὑποσχόμενος ἀντικαθίστασθαι μὲν τοῖς περὶ τὸν δοῦκα Κωνσταντῖνον στρατεύμασιν οὐκ ἔτι ἐᾷ, εἰς δὲ τὴν τῶν Κιλίκων χώραν ἀπαγαγὼν καὶ τὰ τέμπη τῆς Κιλικίας αὐτῷ προβαλόμενος στρατόν τε αὐτῷ ἐξαρτύει καὶ χρήματα δίδωσι, καὶ ὁπλίζει μὲν πρότερον, εἶτ᾽ ἐν καιρῷ μάχεσθαι πρὸς τὸν ἀντίπαλον στρατὸν ταμιεύεται.
units.en: 21. The emperor Diogenes, released from captivity, thought it terrible if he did not take hold of the government again. Sending to towns and lands everywhere, he gathered armies and collected money. When a crowd of the soldiery had already flowed to him, he occupied with his whole army the town famous on every tongue, I mean Amaseia. Learning this, those around the emperor and the Caesar considered whom they should set up against him. They decided to entrust the Roman army to the younger of the Caesar's sons, a man brave with his hand and sharp and admirable in intelligence. He took the forces and went against Diogenes, and when he came near Amaseia he first held his army together and used skirmishes, and contrived in every way either to capture Diogenes or to drive him out of the town. Diogenes, hard pressed, was forced to lead out his forces and draw up against the doux. Both armies met, and very many fell on each side, the generals on both sides fighting nobly. But Diogenes' men fled, when the doux Constantine charged more bravely against those standing in front and pushed back their line. Many of Diogenes' men fell; he himself escaped and shut himself up with a few in a fort. This was the first cause of confidence for those around the emperor Michael, and from then on Diogenes began to fall. He would have been taken at once had not something else happened. There was a man of Armenian descent, deep in judgement and brave with his hand: Koutatarios. He had received one of the greatest commands from Diogenes when he was styled emperor of the Romans, and repaying his gratitude in his misfortune he came to him bringing many soldiers, told him to take heart and promised him the greatest things; he no longer let him face the armies of the doux Constantine, but took him into Cilicia, set the passes of Cilicia before him, equipped an army for him and gave him money; he armed him first, and then bided his time to fight the opposing army at the right moment.
units.note: Close to Psellos (Psell. Coup [6], Psell. Civil [1], [2]), but Khatchatour is 'brave with his hand' instead of 'hostile to us in his leanings'.

units.titel: 22. Letters of amnesty; the trial of Anna Dalassene
units.orig: 22. Ἐν βουλεύμασι τοίνυν καὶ αὖθις τὰ κατὰ τὸν βασιλέα Μιχαὴλ καὶ τὸν καίσαρα, καὶ οἱ τῆς συγκλήτου λογάδες ἠθροίζοντο. καὶ τοῖς μὲν σπείσασθαι πρὸς τὸν Διογένην ἐδόκει καὶ μέρους αὐτῷ τῆς ἀρχῆς παρακεχωρηκέναι, τοῖς δὲ πολεμεῖν καὶ ἔτι δέδοκτο καὶ μηδεμίαν ἀφορμὴν αὐτῷ τῆς εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν εἰσαγωγῆς παρασχεῖν. ἐπράττετο μὲν οὖν πρῶτον τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης, καὶ γράμματα παρὰ τοῦ βασιλέως Μιχαὴλ πρὸς ἐκεῖνον μετὰ πρέσβεων κακῶν ἀμνηστίαν τούτῳ ἐπαγγελλόμενα. ὁ δὲ εἰκότως ὥσπερ ὑβριοπάθειά τις αὐτῷ ἀπηγγέλλετο μηδὲν ὅλως τῶν κακῶν πλημμελήσαντι, εἰς ἀποκρίσεις δὲ καθιστάμενος οὔτε τῆς βασιλείας ἀπείχετο καὶ τὰ μέγιστα διετείνετο ἀδικεῖσθαι. ἀλλὰ τὰ κατὰ τὸν Διογένην ἐπράττετο τῇδε. ὁ δὲ τοῖς καλοῖς βασκαίνων ἀεὶ διωγμόν τινα ἐξήγειρε κατὰ τῶν Κομνηνῶν, καὶ ὅστις λεκτέον. ἄνδρα τινὰ θρασύστομον εὑρηκὼς καὶ ἠκονηκὼς τὴν γλῶτταν αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ ὄφεως κατὰ τῆς γενναίας τούτων μητρὸς καθοπλίζει, συκοφαντίαν συρράψας τινὰ ψεύδους ἔκγονον, καὶ γράμματα συμπλασάμενος ἐξ ἐκείνης πρὸς τὸν Διογένην κομίζει ταῦτα τῷ βασιλεῖ. τῷ δὲ μήθ᾽ ὅστις εἴη ὁ κατήγορος σκοποῦντι μήτε δὴ μένων τοῦ κατηγορουμένου τὸ πρόσωπον, εὐθὺς ξυμβέβηκε μηνιᾶν. ἐντεῦθεν δικαστήριά τε συνεκροτεῖτο καὶ μετάπεμπτος ἡ εὐγενὴς καὶ γενναία καὶ σώφρων ἦν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀνάκτορα. ἡ δὲ ἐφοίτα. ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν βασιλεὺς ᾐδέσθη κοινωνὸς γενέσθαι τοῦ σκέμματος, συνήγοντο δὲ οἱ περὶ τὰ δικαστήρια τῆς κυρίας παρούσης καὶ τοῦ κήρυκος πρὸς τὴν δίκην καλοῦντος. εἴσεισι γοῦν ἡ γενναία καὶ μεγαλόψυχος φαιδρῷ τῷ προσώπῳ, καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα δὲ κρύπτουσα ὑπὸ τὴν χλαμύδα τοῦ πάντων δικαστοῦ ἐξάγει ταύτην ἀθρόον, καὶ σεμνῷ τῷ σχήματι καὶ τῷ βλέμματι πρὸς τοὺς δικαστὰς ἀτενίσασα “οὗτος” ἔφη “δικαστὴς ἐμοῦ τε καὶ ὑμῶν καθίσταται σήμερον, πρὸς ὃν ἀτενίζοντες ψήφους ἐκφέρετε μὴ ἀναξίας τοῦ δικαστοῦ τοῦ εἰδότος τὰ κρύφια.” τὸ γοῦν στερρὸν τοῦ λόγου ἐκεῖνοι ἐνωτισάμενοι θάμβους γεγόνασι μεστοί, καὶ παραιτεῖσθαι τὴν δίκην ἔνιοι ἤρχοντο βδελυττόμενοι τὴν συκοφαντίαν· ἤδη γὰρ διέλαμψεν ἡ ἀλήθεια ὡς πυρσὸς ὑπ᾽ αἰθάλῃ κρυπτόμενος. ἀλλ᾽ οἱ μὲν τὸν θεῖον φόβον ταῖς καρδίαις ἐντρέφοντες καὶ πνεῦμα σωτηρίας ὠδίνοντες οὕτως, οἱ δὲ πάντα χαρίζεσθαι τοῖς κρατοῦσι βουλόμενοι δεινοί τινες δικασταὶ καθεστήκεισαν. ἐπεὶ δὲ οὐχ οἷόν τε ἦν ἀποδείκνυσθαι τὴν συκοφαντίαν καὶ τὸν κρατοῦντα ᾐδοῦντο, μᾶλλον δὲ πρὸ ἐκείνου τὸν τὸν δόλον συρράψαντα, οὐκ ἀποφαίνονται μέν, εἰς πρόληψιν δὲ τὸ πρᾶγμα ἐνάγουσι. βαβαὶ τῆς ἀσυνεσίας! ποία πρόληψις ὦ ἐμβρόντητοι! εἶπεν ἄν τις πρὸς αὐτοὺς θαρραλέως, ὁπηνίκα ὁ μὲν κατήγορος ἀναιδὴν φθέγγεται, ὁ δὲ φεύγων γενναίως τὰς κατηγορίας ἀποσκευάζεται, καὶ ὁ μὲν ἀγύρτης ἐστὶ καὶ ὀβολοῦ πιπράσκων τὴν δίκην εἰ δέοι, ὁ δὲ πάσης ὑποψίας ἀνώτερος καὶ πρὸς αὐτὴν μικροῦ δεῖν ἐρυθριῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν. τουτὶ μὲν τὸ συνέδριον οὕτω πως διελέλυτο, μικροῦ δεῖν ἐοικὸς τῷ τοῦ Καϊάφα· ἡ δὲ σὺν τοῖς παισὶν εἰς τὴν τοῦ πριγκίπου ἐξορίζεται νῆσον.
units.en: 22. So once again the affairs of the emperor Michael and the Caesar were in counsel, and the chosen men of the senate were gathered. Some thought they should make a treaty with Diogenes and grant him part of the government; others still decided on war and on giving him no opening to return to the throne. The business of peace was pursued first, and letters from the emperor Michael were sent to him with envoys, promising him an amnesty for wrongs. He, naturally, took it almost as an insult that this was announced to him, as if he had done wrong, when he had done no wrong at all; and in his answers he neither kept away from the throne and maintained that he was suffering the greatest injustice. But this is how things went for Diogenes. He who always envies good things stirred up a persecution against the Komnenoi, and it must be told how. Having found a man of bold tongue, and sharpened his tongue like a serpent's, he armed him against their noble mother, stitching together a calumny, a child of falsehood; and forging letters from her to Diogenes, he brought them to the emperor. The emperor, considering neither who the accuser was nor waiting for the face of the accused, at once grew angry. So a court was assembled, and the well-born, noble and chaste lady was summoned to the palace; and she came. The emperor was ashamed to take part in the matter, but the members of the court gathered, the lady was present, and the herald called her to judgement. The noble and great-hearted lady came in with a radiant face, and, hiding under her cloak the icon of the Judge of all, she suddenly brought it out, and looking at the judges with a solemn bearing and gaze she said: 'This is the judge, of me and of you, today: look at him and give verdicts not unworthy of the Judge who knows what is hidden.' Hearing the firmness of her words they were filled with amazement, and some began to excuse themselves from the case, loathing the calumny; for the truth was already shining out like a torch hidden under soot. So those who fostered the fear of God in their hearts and were in labour with the spirit of salvation; but those who wished to gratify the powerful in everything were terrible judges. Since the calumny could not be proved, and they feared the ruler, or rather, more than him, the man who had stitched the plot together, they did not give a verdict, but brought the matter to a presumption. Oh, the folly! What presumption, you thunderstruck men! one might boldly have said to them, when the accuser speaks shamelessly, and the defendant nobly rebuts the charges; when he is a charlatan who would sell justice for an obol if need be, and she is above all suspicion and all but blushes before the truth itself. That council was dissolved in this way, almost like that of Caiaphas; and she with her children was exiled to the island of Prinkipos.
units.note: The mother is Anna Dalassene, mother of the Komnenoi and grandmother of the author's wife Anna Komnene; the man 'who always envies good things' is the Devil, the accuser unnamed. The trial is known only from Bryennios and belongs to the family history of the Komnenoi. Meineke's apparatus suggests a verb is missing after 'envoys'.

sections.titel: The civil war and the blinding (1071–1072)
sections.blurb: Andronikos, obedient to his father, through the Cilician passes; Crispin's charge; Khatchatour naked in a thicket and his hidden jewel; Adana surrendered; Andronikos weeps, shares his table with the captive, and writes to his father the Caesar to stop the blinding. It happens anyway.

units.orig: 23. Καὶ τὰ μὲν κατ᾽ αὐτοὺς ὧδε ἐπράττετο. ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς Μιχαὴλ καὶ οἱ περὶ τὸν καίσαρα ἀπογνόντες τὰ πρὸς εἰρήνην ἐπεὶ ἔφθη ὁ δοὺξ Κωνσταντῖνος ὁ τῷ Διογένει συμπλακεὶς καὶ τοῦτον ἡττήσας, ὃν υἱὸν εἶναι τοῦ καίσαρος δεύτερον ὁ λόγος ἡρμήνευσεν ἄνωθεν, παλινοστῆσαι πρὸς τὸ Βυζάντιον, ἐσκέπτοντο ὅπως ἂν τὰ κατὰ τὸν Διογένην διάθωνται. ἐδεδίεσαν γὰρ μή πως ἀδείας πάλιν ἐκεῖνος δραξάμενος στρατεύματά τε συναγείρῃ τῶν πρώην πλείονα, καὶ χρήματα τῶν ἐκ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας χωρῶν εἰσπράξηται καὶ δυσμαχώτερος κατασταίη. εὐθὺς οὖν ὁ καῖσαρ μετακαλεῖται τὸν υἱὸν Κωνσταντῖνον, καὶ αὖθις τὰς δυνάμεις ἀναλαμβάνειν καὶ κατὰ τοῦ Διογένους χωρεῖν παρεκελεύετο. τοῦ δὲ παραιτουμένου, ὁ πρεσβύτερος τῶν τοῦ καίσαρος υἱῶν μετεκαλεῖτο Ἀνδρόνικος καὶ ἐκελεύετο ἀπιέναι. ὁ δὲ εἴπερ τις ἄλλος ὑπήκοος ὢν πατρὶ εὐθὺς ἕτοιμος ἦν πρὸς τὸ ἔργον. συνταξάμενος οὖν αὐθημερὸν τῷ βασιλεῖ καὶ τῷ καίσαρι τὸν πορθμὸν διεπεραιοῦτο τὸν Χαλκηδόνιον. καὶ ἓξ ἡμέρας διατρίψας περὶ τὴν Χαλκηδόνα ὅσον τὰ ἐπιτήδειά οἱ τὰ πρὸς τὴν ἐκστρατείαν γενέσθαι, ἐκεῖθεν ἀπάρας περιῄει τὴν ἕω καὶ τὰς δυνάμεις συνέλεγε. καὶ θᾶττον ἁπάσας συλλέξας ξὺν αὐταῖς ἐχώρει πρὸς τὴν Κιλίκων. σκοπὸν δ᾽ ἔθετο πρῶτον εἰς μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν γνώμην μεθαρμόσασθαι τὸ στρατόπεδον· ἐπεὶ δὲ τοῦτο αὐτῷ ἐξεγένετο ἑκάστῳ προσφερομένῳ ἐπιεικῶς καὶ πρὸς πάντα μεθαρμοζομένῳ οἰκείως, δεύτερον σκοπὸν τίθεται τοὺς πολεμίους λαθεῖν καὶ τὰ στενὰ τῆς Κιλικίας διελθεῖν πρὸ τοῦ τὸν Διογένην αἰσθέσθαι τῆς τούτου ἐφόδου. γίνεται οὖν καὶ τοῦτο κατὰ τὰ βεβουλευμένα, καὶ τὴν στενὴν καὶ ἀπόκρημνον διελθόντες οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἀνδρόνικον ἀθρόοι τοῖς περὶ βασιλέα τὸν Διογένην ἐπιφαίνονται.
units.en: 23. So it went with them. The emperor Michael and the Caesar's party, giving up on peace, since the doux Constantine, who had engaged Diogenes and beaten him (the Caesar's second son, as my account explained above), had got back to Byzantium first, considered how they should deal with Diogenes. For they feared that he might again seize the chance to gather more armies than before, collect money from the lands of Antioch, and become harder to fight. At once the Caesar called his son Constantine and urged him to take up the forces again and march against Diogenes. When he declined, the elder of the Caesar's sons, Andronikos, was called and told to go. He, as obedient to his father as anyone, was at once ready for the task. Having taken leave of the emperor and the Caesar that same day, he crossed the strait of Chalcedon; and after spending six days near Chalcedon, as long as it took to make ready what he needed for the campaign, he set out from there, went round the East and gathered the forces. Having quickly gathered them all, he marched with them towards Cilicia. His first aim was to bring the army to one and the same mind; and when he had achieved this by treating each man fairly and adapting himself to all as a friend, he set as his second aim to escape the enemy's notice and get through the narrows of Cilicia before Diogenes perceived his approach. This too happened as planned, and having passed the narrow and precipitous way, Andronikos' men suddenly appeared before the emperor Diogenes' men.
units.note: Psellos' chapter on Andronikos (Psell. Civil [4]), with the family's details: Constantine declined, Andronikos obeyed his father. 'The emperor Diogenes': Bryennios keeps his title throughout.

units.orig: 24. Αἰσθόμενος δὲ καὶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῆς τούτων ἐφόδου ἐξῆγε καὶ αὐτὸς τὰς δυνάμεις, τῷ Χουτατουρίῳ Ἀρμενίῳ, ὃν φθάσας ἐδήλωσεν ἄνωθεν ὁ λόγος, τὴν τοῦ πολέμου δεδωκὼς ἐξουσίαν καὶ πάντα τὸν στρατὸν μικροῦ δεῖν αὐτῷ ὑποτάξας. τοὺς πεζοὺς οὖν οὗτος καὶ ἱππεῖς ἐπαγόμενος τοὺς ἐπικαίρους τῶν τόπων καταλαβεῖν ἔσπευδεν. ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐλπίδων ἐσφάλη, τοῦ δομεστίκου τῶν σχολῶν Ἀνδρονίκου προκατασχόντος αὐτούς. ἀπογνοὺς οὖν τούτου ἀντιμέτωπον τὴν ἰδίαν φάλαγγα τῇ τῶν ἐναντίων ἵστησιν· ἀντικαθίσταται δὲ πρὸς τοῦτον καὶ ὁ Ἀνδρόνικος. καὶ τοῦ μὲν μέσου τῆς φάλαγγος αὐτὸς ἦν ἐξηγούμενος, τοῦ εὐωνύμου δὲ κέρατος ὁ Φράγγος Κρισπῖνος, τοῦ δεξιοῦ δ᾽ ἕτερός τις τῶν ὑπὸ τὸν Ἀνδρόνικον τεταγμένων. ἀλλὰ πρὶν ἢ τὸν συνασπισμὸν γενέσθαι καὶ εἰς χεῖρας ἀλλήλων ἰέναι, ὁ Φράγγος δύσνους ὢν πάλαι τῷ βασιλεῖ Ῥωμανῷ καὶ μῆνιν κατ᾽ αὐτοῦ τρέφων, τὸ τῶν ἐναντίων ἱππικὸν θεασάμενος καὶ τῷ Ἀνδρονίκῳ προειπὼν τὴν κατ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐξέλασιν, ἀπὸ ῥυτῆρος σὺν τοῖς ἀμφ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐξελαύνει τὸν ἵππον. ἰσχυρᾶς οὖν τῆς προσβολῆς γενομένης φεύγουσιν οἱ περὶ τὸν Χουτατούριον. οἱ δὲ κατόπιν διώκοντες πολλοὺς μὲν ἀνῄρουν πολλοὺς δὲ καὶ ἐζώγρουν. τοῦ γοῦν ἱππικοῦ οὕτω διασκεδασθέντος καὶ ἡ φάλαγξ ἡ πεζική, δείσασα μὴ κυκλωθεῖσα διακοπείη, τὰ νῶτα δοῦσα καὶ αὐτὴ πρὸς φυγὴν ἔκλινεν. ὅσοι μὲν οὖν ταῖς φάραγξι καὶ ταῖς λόχμαις εἰσέδυσαν, διεσώθησαν, τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν οἱ μὲν ἔπεσον οἱ δὲ ἐζωγρήθησαν. καὶ ἡ μὲν τοῦ Διογένους φάλαγξ οὕτω διελέλυτο καὶ διεσκέδαστο, τροπαιοφόρῳ δ᾽ ἐπανελθόντι τῷ Ἀνδρονίκῳ πρὸς τὴν σκηνὴν καὶ μετ᾽ εὐφροσύνης τὰ χαριστήρια θύοντι καὶ ἕτερον ἐπῆλθεν εὐτύχημα. ἱππεὺς γάρ τις ἧκεν ὡς τάχιστα πρὸς αὐτὸν τῶν πολεμίων ἄγων τινὰ καὶ τὸν στρατηγὸν ἐζήτει θεάσασθαι. ὁ δὲ τῆς σκηνῆς προκύψας ἑώρα πρᾶγμα πολλὴν αὐτῷ θυμηδίαν παρέχον, τὸν Χουτατούριον πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀγόμενον δέσμιον. οὗτος γὰρ ἐν τῷ φεύγειν τοῦ ἵππου διωλισθηκότος, ὡς ἔλεγε, λόχμην τε εἰσέδυ τινὰ καὶ λανθάνειν ἔσπευδεν. ὡς δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν διωκόντων καταφανὴς γέγονε καὶ συλληφθεὶς ἔμελλεν ἀναιρεῖσθαι, ἐλιπάρει τὸν ζωγρήσαντα. ὡς δὲ δακρύοντα οὗτος τὸν ἄνδρα τεθέαται, τὴν ἐσθῆτα ἀποδυσάμενος καὶ γυμνὸν ἐπὶ τὴν λόχμην ἀφεὶς ἀπῄει. εἶτα δὴ ἄλλος αὐτὸν γυμνὸν κατιδὼν ὑπὸ τὴν λόχμην κρυπτόμενον ὥρμησεν ἀναιρεῖν, ὁ δὲ ὅστις εἴη ἐφθέγγετο καὶ πρὸς τὸν στρατηγὸν ἀπαχθῆναι παρεκάλει. κἀκεῖνος ταχέως τοῦτον ἐπὶ τοῦ ἵππου θεὶς πρὸς τὸν Ἀνδρόνικον ἀπεκόμιζεν. ὃν ἐκεῖνος ἐκ τῆς σκηνῆς ἰδὼν γυμνὸν ἐπαγόμενον ἐξῄει τε τῆς σκηνῆς καὶ ἵλεῳ τῷ ὄμματι τοῦτον καθυπεβλέπετο. παραστείλας οὖν τὴν αὐτοῦ γύμνωσιν περιβολῇ στρατηγῷ πρεπούσῃ γενναίῳ ἐν ἀδέσμῳ ἐτήρει φυλακῇ. ἀγασθεὶς δὲ ὁ Χουτατούριος τῆς περὶ αὐτὸν φιλοφροσύνης τοῦ Ἀνδρονίκου, λίθον τινὰ τῶν πολυτίμων ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ κρυβέντα περὶ τὴν λόχμην ἐν ᾗ ἑάλω αὐτῷ φανεροῖ, καὶ πέμψαι ξὺν αὐτῷ ἀξιοῖ τοὺς ἀποκομίζοντας. καὶ δὴ πέμπονται, καὶ κομίζουσι θέαμα τοῖς ὁρῶσιν ἰδεῖν. μεγέθει γὰρ ἦν σχεδὸν ὑπὲρ ἅπαντας λίθους, λαμπρότητι δὲ τοὺς διαυγεῖς ἅπαντας ὑπερέλαμπεν. ὃν ὁ Ἀνδρόνικος τῇ βασιλίδι Μαρίᾳ δῶρον προσήνεγκεν ὕστερον.
units.en: 24. When the emperor perceived their approach, he too led out his forces, having given the command of the war to Khoutatourios the Armenian, whom my account has already made known, and put almost the whole army under him. He, bringing infantry and cavalry, hurried to occupy the key places; but he was disappointed in his hopes, since the domestikos of the scholai Andronikos had occupied them first. Giving this up, he set his own line facing the enemy's; and Andronikos too took his stand against him. He himself led the centre of the line, the Frank Crispin the left wing, and one of the officers under Andronikos the right. But before the shields met and they came to blows, the Frank, long ill-disposed to the emperor Romanos and nursing wrath against him, saw the enemy cavalry, told Andronikos beforehand of his charge against them, and rode out at full gallop with his men. The attack was so strong that Khoutatourios' men fled; the pursuers killed many and took many alive. With the cavalry thus scattered, the infantry line too, fearing to be surrounded and cut to pieces, turned its back and gave way to flight. Those who crept into the ravines and thickets escaped; of the rest some fell and some were taken. So Diogenes' line was broken up and scattered; and when Andronikos had returned to his tent as a bearer of trophies and was joyfully offering thanks, another piece of good fortune came to him. A horseman came to him in haste bringing one of the enemy and asked to see the general. He, leaning out of his tent, saw a thing that gave him great delight: Khoutatourios being brought to him in chains. For in his flight, when his horse slipped, as he said, he had crept into a thicket and was trying to hide. When he was spotted by the pursuers, caught and about to be killed, he begged his captor; and he, seeing the man in tears, stripped off his clothes and went away leaving him naked in the thicket. Then another, seeing him naked hiding under the thicket, set out to kill him; but he said who he was and begged to be taken to the general. The man quickly put him on his horse and took him to Andronikos. Andronikos, seeing him brought naked, came out of his tent and looked on him with a kindly eye. He covered his nakedness with clothing fitting a noble general and kept him in guard without chains. Khoutatourios, delighted with Andronikos' kindness to him, revealed to him a precious stone he had hidden near the thicket where he was taken, and asked him to send men with him to bring it. They were sent, and brought back a sight to behold: in size it was almost beyond all stones, and in brilliance it outshone all clear ones. Andronikos later gave it as a present to the empress Maria.
units.note: Again from Psellos (Psell. Civil [7]–[9]), with the family's additions: the order of battle, Crispin's grudge against Romanos, and Khatchatour's hidden jewel, given to the empress Maria of Alania, Michael VII's wife.

units.titel: 25. Adana surrenders; Andronikos protests the blinding
units.orig: 25. Ὁ δὲ Διογένης καὶ τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῷ κατόπιν ἀρμένων οὐ κατεγίνωσκεν, ἀλλὰ τοὺς περὶ αὐτὸν ὑπερώννυε καὶ ἐλπίδας ὑπέτεινεν ὡς ἀφιξομένης αὐτίκα δὴ μάλα Περσικῆς συμμαχίας. διεπρεσβεύετο δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὸν Κρισπῖνον πειρώμενος αὐτοῦ τὸ βάρβαρον φρόνημα διεγεῖραι κατὰ τοῦ Ἀνδρονίκου. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο γνοὺς Ἀνδρόνικος καὶ θωπευτικώτερον ἐντετυχηκὼς τῷ Κρισπίνῳ τὴν ἐκείνου πρεσβείαν ἀπέδειξεν ἄπρακτον. ἀπράκτου δὲ τῆς πρεσβείας ἀποδειχθείσης καὶ τοῦ ἐκ Περσίδος συμμαχικοῦ ἔτι μέλλοντος, οἱ περὶ τὸν Διογένην ἀπογνόντες τῷ Ἀνδρονίκῳ συνθέμενοι καὶ πίστεις τοῦ μὴ παθεῖν εἰληφότες αὐτόν τε τὸν βασιλέα παραδιδόασι καὶ τὸ φρούριον. οἱ δὲ περὶ τὸν Δούκα Ἀνδρόνικον αὐτὸν συλλαβόντες τὴν ἁλουργίδα αὐτὸν ἀποδύσαντες, τὸ μοναδικὸν ἐπενδύουσι σχῆμα, καὶ οὕτω τοῦ φρουρίου ἐξαγαγόντες πρὸς τὸν Ἀνδρόνικον μετὰ πλείστης ὅτι τῆς περιχαρείας ἀπάγουσιν. ὁ δὲ τῆς τύχης αὐτὸν οἰκτείρας ἐδάκρυσε καὶ δεξιὰν ἐμβαλὼν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀπάγει σκηνὴν καὶ τραπέζης αὐτῷ κοινωνεῖ. ἦν οὖν ἄμεινον μέχρι τούτου στῆναι τῷ ἀνδρὶ τὰ τῆς δυστυχίας· ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἦν αὐτῷ διαδρᾶναι τοῦ φθόνου τὰ βέλεμνα. οἱ γὰρ περὶ τὸν βασιλέα Μιχαὴλ πρόφασιν ὥσπερ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας τὴν πρὸς ἐκεῖνον πλασάμενοι εὔνοιαν, δείσαντες ὡς ἔφησαν μή τι καὶ διαμηχανήσαιτο ὁ Διογένης καὶ πάλιν ἀφορμὴ πραγμάτων τῷ βασιλεῖ γένοιτο, ἐντέλλονταί τινι διὰ γραμμάτων ἐπὶ τοῦ καιροῦ δυναστεύοντι ἐκκόψαι τούτῳ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς. ὃ δὴ καὶ γενόμενον μεγάλως ἠνίασε τὸν Ἀνδρόνικον, καὶ μᾶλλον ὅτι καὶ πειρασθεὶς διασώσασθαι τοῦτον οὐ δεδύνητο, τῶν περὶ τὸν βασιλέα σφοδρότερον ἐγκειμένων. ἐπέστειλε δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τὸν καίσαρα, παρακαλῶν αὐτὸν μὴ συγχωρῆσαι τελεσθῆναι τοιοῦτον ἀνοσιούργημα, ἢ μὴν τῆς θείας ἐκδέχεσθαι δίκης τὴν ψῆφον οὐκ εἰς μακρὰν ἀπαντήσουσαν. ὁ μὲν οὖν ταῦτα, οἱ δὲ τὰ γράμματα δεξάμενοι ἐκτυφλοῦσί τε τοῦτον, καὶ εἰς ὃ ἱδρύσατο φροντιστήριον ἐν τῇ νήσῳ Πρώτῃ ἐκπέμπουσι. βραχὺ δέ τι ἐπιβιοὺς μετὰ τὴν τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν στέρησιν ἐτελεύτησεν, ἐπὶ τρισὶν ἔτεσι τὴν βασιλείαν Ῥωμαίων ἰθύνας. τοιοῦτον ἔσχε τέλος τὰ κατὰ τὸν Διογένην.
units.en: 25. Diogenes, though his affairs had gone wrong for him, did not give up, but strengthened those with him and held out hopes that Persian help would come very soon. He also sent envoys to Crispin, trying to stir up his barbarian pride against Andronikos. But Andronikos learned of it, met Crispin in a more flattering way, and made the embassy fruitless. When the embassy had proved fruitless and the help from Persia was still to come, Diogenes' men gave up hope, came to terms with Andronikos, received pledges that they would suffer nothing, and handed over the emperor himself and the fortress. Andronikos Doukas' men seized him, stripped him of the purple, put on him the monk's habit, and so led him out of the fortress and brought him to Andronikos with the greatest possible joy. He, pitying his fortune, wept, gave him his right hand, took him to his own tent and shared his table with him. It would have been better for the man's misfortunes to stop there; but he could not escape the arrows of envy. For those around the emperor Michael, pretending goodwill towards him as a cover for their own desire, and fearing, as they said, that Diogenes might contrive something and again give the emperor trouble, ordered by letter someone then in power to cut out his eyes. This, when it was done, grieved Andronikos greatly, and all the more because he had tried to save him and could not, those around the emperor pressing harder. He had also written to his father the Caesar, begging him not to allow such an unholy deed to be carried out, or else to expect the sentence of divine justice to come upon them before long. So he; but those who had received the letters blinded him and sent him to the monastery he had founded on the island of Prote. He lived a little while after the loss of his eyes and died, having ruled the empire of the Romans for three years. Such was the end of the story of Diogenes.
units.note: The family's defence. Andronikos Doukas, whose rearguard broke at Manzikert and who took Romanos at Adana, weeps, protests the blinding and writes to his father the Caesar to stop it. Psellos: 'the more devoted' ordered it, and Michael did not know (Psell. Civil [10], [11]). Attaleiates: an order from the emperor, and the bishops' oath broken (Att. Blind. [2], [4]). The author wrote this for Andronikos' daughter, the empress Eirene Doukaina. Meineke queries ἐπερρώννυε and τι παθεῖν.
